A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisionLaw, with matching methods and substantial shared results. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–H, which provide newly available documentation and evidence.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on six synthetic scenes and two real-world scenes, including quantitative comparisons, temporal generalization, and a decoupling ablation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds transfer experiments, optimizer comparisons, and supplementary quantitative and qualitative analyses.

M1.justification: The core bilevel framework, alternating-then-joint constitutive evolution, and visual loss remain unchanged. Section 4.3.4 adds a tested adaptation replacing gradient-based lower-level parameter optimization with differential evolution. Newly documented prompts and Particle-GS binding do not independently establish changes to the original method.

E1.justification: The original six synthetic and two real-world scenes remain. v2 adds image-to-4D and 3D-to-4D generation on new assets, transfers inferred laws between scenes, and tests initial velocities of 0.5 and 1.5 times the original velocity (Figures 6, 12, and 13). These substantially broaden coverage beyond reconstruction and temporal extrapolation.

E2.justification: NCLaw, previously discussed only as related work, becomes an evaluated comparator in Table 1 and the trajectory comparisons in Figure 10. PAC-NeRF, NeuMA, and Spring-Gaus remain in their corresponding original comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled optimizer comparisons using differential-evolution populations of 5 and 10 with 10 lower-level iterations, gravity-only transfer evaluations, velocity perturbations, and viewwise PSNR/variance evaluation. It also reports linear-isotropic initialization in Section 4.1.1 and Appendix A.1 instead of v1's fixed-corotated initialization, although Appendix E contradictorily retains the old setting. The original temporal split and five-iteration decoupling ablation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The temporal generalization experiment and original decoupling curves are retained, with v1 Figure 6 becoming v2 Figure 7. Added analyses examine viewpoint overfitting, time-resolved trajectory errors, cross-scene and velocity robustness, NeuMA's numerical divergence during transfer, gradient-free optimization, and decoupling's runtime-versus-accuracy tradeoff.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1 newly specifies seed IDs 0–4, and Figure 11(b) adds PSNR variance across viewpoints. Both versions already report five independent seeded runs and mean curves with minimum–maximum shading for the decoupling ablation. The additions disclose seeds and quantify viewpoint variability; they do not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains every original entry, including VisionLaw's average Chamfer distance of 1.65, and adds NCLaw's average of 12.86. v2 adds extensive transfer, trajectory, optimizer, and runtime results; Table 2 reports RGB losses of 10.73 versus 7.14 at 11,343 versus 11,405 seconds without versus with decoupling. Visual-fidelity summaries also change, with v2 explicitly reporting non-training-view averages; these should not be interpreted as established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Equation 3 corrects the transmittance product's upper limit from i to i−1. Appendices D and E additionally formalize standard MPM updates and classical elastic/plastic constitutive laws. The main bilevel optimization formulation remains essentially intact, without new theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: inferring interpretable constitutive laws and material parameters through bilevel optimization, improving search through decoupled evolution, and supporting generalizable physical interaction. Consolidating the contribution bullets and adding supporting experiments do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v2 extends the physical-inductive-bias interpretation to viewpoint overfitting and transfer instability, and argues for applicability to non-differentiable simulation through gradient-free optimization while acknowledging its computational overhead. Appendix F newly identifies extensive simulation and parameter optimization as a practical limitation and proposes preliminary screening as future work.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantial details missing from the supplied v1: Particle-GS binding, parent/offspring counts, the default evolution schedule, lower-level iteration counts, simulation resolutions, and frame subsampling. Appendices G and H provide full prompts and inferred Python constitutive laws for all eight original scenes. The abstract also adds an implementation repository address.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including differential evolution by Storn and Price, Blickhan's spring-mass model, and recent scientific-discovery and simulation work; the Mip-NeRF reference is removed. Related-work discussion receives limited expansion, while the central positioning relative to predefined laws, neural constitutive models, and SGA remains.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Related Work moves to Appendix C, four contribution bullets become two, the MPM explanation expands, and the experimental discussion separates dynamics consistency, visual fidelity, and several generalization analyses into numbered subsections. Much of the core method description remains recognizable despite this structural revision.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. Figure 1 becomes a comparative overview, Figure 4 gains a constitutive-code panel, and the original visual-metric figure is reorganized across Figures 3 and 11. Existing ablation plots are rearranged, and numerous transfer, diagnostic, and runtime displays are added, including Table 2.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's gaps in reproducibility, inspectability, and support for cross-scene transfer. Appendices A, G, and H disclose settings, prompts, and inferred laws, while Figures 6, 12, and 13 provide concrete transfer evidence beyond the original temporal tests. Added baseline, viewpoint, and runtime analyses strengthen assessment without relying on improved headline scores. The conflicting initialization descriptions remain a reproducibility weakness, but the substantive evidence and documentation gains outweigh it.
